issues.description: The problem specification and UML expect a StockIngredient constructor with three parameters (String name, int price, int quantity), and the solution implements a three-argument constructor. However, the template repository provides only a four-parameter constructor StockIngredient(String, int, int, boolean). This mismatch will confuse students when they try to instantiate StockIngredient as described in the task (and as the tests/solution expect) and may block them from following examples or creating SealSaloon.acceptSupplyDelivery that uses new StockIngredient(name, price, quantity).
issues.suggestedFix: Make the template's StockIngredient class provide the three-argument constructor expected by the problem and solution. For example, add a public StockIngredient(String name, int price, int quantity) constructor that delegates to the existing constructor (e.g., calling this(name, price, quantity, true)), or change the existing constructor to a three-argument signature. This keeps the template consistent with the UML, problem description, and solution code.

issues.description: The problem statement and class diagram specify a StockIngredient constructor with signature StockIngredient(String, int, int), but the template repository only provides a constructor StockIngredient(String, int, int, boolean). The solution repository implements the 3-argument constructor. This mismatch in constructor signatures (and thus the expected way to instantiate StockIngredient) creates confusion for students: the problem text and solution expect a 3-arg constructor while the provided starter code requires an extra boolean parameter.
issues.suggestedFix: Add the 3-argument constructor StockIngredient(String name, int price, int quantity) to the template (or adjust the problem description). Implement it to delegate to or replicate the validation logic of the existing constructor (e.g., call the 4-arg constructor with a default strictValidation value) so the API matches the class diagram and the solution.
